items.question: What do you think matters most in someone's ability to become an AI researcher?
items.object: The abilities and training needed to become an AI researcher
items.answer: I think really the most important thing is there are a lot of researchers who just started out without a formal training in machine learning or AI research. We've very much believed in training people up to do this. I think the real hard thing is the ability to creatively solve problems and think outside of the box. It's not so much, you know, you have to do a PhD, even though that does bring a valuable skill set.

items.question: How do you see trading as preparation for AI research?
items.object: Trading as preparation for AI research
items.answer: With trading in particular, I mean, I don't know that it's that special of a profession. Like, I kind of think of it as, you know, we've had great mathematicians join, we already had great physicists join, but trading is something where it's very unhackable. You can't kind of cheat the real world, right? You know, it's a hard metric to optimize. And there's also a lot of characteristics, like it's a field where attention to detail really matters. And, you know, it's kind of the brutal hard optimization and squeezing out the juice of a system. And some of those skills transfer over.

items.question: How do you think someone entering AI research should develop research taste?
items.object: Developing research taste through replication
items.answer: I think it's a little bit overrated. It is something you have to develop, but the best mechanism I've found for developing that is really just replication. So, I think you should take papers that you really look up to and just try to fully replicate it. Back in 2018, there is, you know, like ResNet, there were Pixel CNNs, and I learned so much just trying to replicate the training curves exactly, get to the exact amount of, you know, like training loss or perplexity that the papers hinted towards. You just see a lot of techniques, right, that people don't really kind of talk about, but once you dive in a couple of layers deeper, you learn those techniques.

items.question: How do you think the ability to grade work affects where reinforcement learning can succeed?
items.object: Reinforcement learning in subjective versus objective fields
items.answer: Yeah, I mean, I think RL's traditionally had headwinds when it's come to fields that, you know, it's more subjective than objective. So, if you kind of think of, you know, one example of this is creative writing, where you could take two pieces of creative writing and two experts can have wildly different opinions. So, it's these fields where things are hard to grade, where RL has the least amount of ability to kind of go and directly apply there. I know a lot of people are developing techniques to apply RL in these settings, but for now, it's just where there's cold hard truth, things like math and computer science, where you can prove it correctly or wrong. That's where you kind of see it really taking off.

items.question: How do you think evaluation of increasingly capable AI models should evolve beyond programming contests?
items.object: Real-world evaluation of increasingly capable AI models
items.answer: I feel like a lot of it centers in on interfacing with the real world. And when we've thought about how to evolve past things like programming contests in the past, I think a lot of the initial direction we took was you should move it to real-world research, right? And we've seen that the models, they've gotten a lot better at just discovering novel theorems and pushing the frontiers of hard sciences. But even today, right? That's no longer a surprise. I think, like, we almost take it for granted now that these models can solve very difficult problems. They can make contributions and even draw relationships between fields that are novel and insightful. So, we think of coding co-working as really a domain for that, that tests whether our models can learn in high-context settings and in real-world long-horizon settings.

items.question: Why do you disagree with the claim that LLM pre-training is dead?
items.object: Scaling laws and the claim that LLM pre-training is dead
items.answer: I firmly believe in exponent being on the exponential and in scaling laws. So, I think any of these bear takes, I fairly strongly disagree with. You know, when it comes to pre-training is dead, I mean, I think the funny thing is this narrative only started spreading more widely after, let's say, the last one or two years or so. In many times in the history of developing LLMs, people have been saying this, right? And there've always been some bottlenecks that people will—well, you can't scale past this because of this bottleneck. And we've always found some kind of technique, whether it be better engineering or some new research insight that helps you break past the boundary. And so, I think it's just more and more of the same, right? Like more careful research engineering, more careful data engineering, more careful scaling. And it always unlocks that next ability to scale further. So, it's held for almost 10 orders of magnitude, but there's no reason it should not keep holding.

items.question: How do you view OpenAI’s decision to pursue reasoning when pre-training plus post-training already seemed so promising?
items.object: OpenAI’s bet on reasoning and O1
items.answer: Well, yeah, I mean, I think of reasoning as one of the biggest examples of this. And the first breakthrough that we launched to the world here was O1, but it wasn't easy to get that off the ground because the world we were living in back then, it was one where pre-training plus post-training, right? That felt like such a promising paradigm. And so, even at a company like OpenAI, you would have people ask naturally, why do something when you have a machine that works? And fundamentally, it's to the credit of Yakub, Ilya, many of the people who really had conviction and vision in the space that we started pushing on this in earnest. And even then, it took a lot of steering to get the whole company behind this as a fundamental bet.

items.question: How do you think research direction at OpenAI benefits from both managers’ judgment and individual researchers’ convictions?
items.object: Top-down and bottom-up research direction at OpenAI
items.answer: You know, what's really cool about OpenAI is research, it feels like a meritocracy. So, oftentimes the research managers are the people who have done the best research in the past. And so I think a lot of steering can come top-down, right? Like if your manager says, "Hey, you know, I'm really convinced this is the path forward." Generally people will take that into heavy consideration, right? It's like, you know, this person who you've respected for their research taste and execution for so long is now very excited by this idea. It's definitely something that people take into account. So, I think there's good top-down steering. At the same time, I think one really cool thing about OpenAI is there are bottom-up elements. We like to be convinced that we're wrong, right? And someone can just come with cold, hard evidence. And many things like that have turned into core parts of our research roadmap. Just things that no one was really trying to steer, but some researcher on the ground had a heavy conviction in. And that's also a really good big delight to see.

items.question: How do you think OpenAI’s research roadmap should adapt as model development around you keeps improving?
items.object: OpenAI’s research roadmap and how it is reassessed
items.answer: Yeah, so I think the thing is the high-level research roadmap should be stable, right? I think people need something to ground in. People need to see a path to what we're building. And I've been very happy that we stayed the course for a while. But the implementation details can change over time, right? And I think it's important to, like, the sequencing will matter, right? The relative resourcing will matter. And the exact steps on the ground will matter. So, what we do is, I think we have points in time that force us to reconsider these things. So, one example is when we do compute. One of the parts of the job is just figuring out how to allocate compute projects. And it's a time to kind of question, are we really putting compute to use in people's use at the highest priority bets?

items.question: How do you think about the high-level structure of OpenAI’s research roadmap?
items.object: The high-level structure of OpenAI’s research roadmap
items.answer: Well, yeah, I mean, at the very highest level, we have an org that focuses on pre-training, which is giving models a lot of world knowledge. We focus on RL, teaching the models how to reason with that knowledge, how to chain the little insights together. And then finally, alignment and post-training. And we're always looking at both how to scale the mainline in each of these domains and also new bets that fundamentally unlock either different scaling properties or more aggressive scaling properties.

items.question: How do you judge a researcher's potential to make an impact at OpenAI?
items.object: Assessing a researcher's potential
items.answer: It's a hard problem before someone comes to OpenAI. I think that's genuinely true. I think for a lot of the best research managers, they work with so many researchers over time where you kind of develop an intuition, like, the things that they say, the ideas that they bring up, do they hit the same mark or are they the things that you would be thinking about personally too? And so there's this gut check of, does their intuition match the same intuition that you have? But it is really hard to tell out of the gate. Usually in, let's say, six months to a year, it's pretty clear who has the strongest trajectory and who's going to make a lot of impact. So, honestly, I think it's a hard problem, but just having seen a lot of people go through research development at OpenAI, you develop an intuition for who's more peppy in different areas.

items.answer: One thing to just mention there is not every researcher is the same. I think there's a lot of different types of impact. items.question: Why do you think high benchmark scores can fail to reflect how well a model generalizes?
items.object: Benchmark maxing and model generalization
items.answer: I mean, I think there is this phenomenon. Internally, I'm not sure if this is an externally used word, but, yeah, just like bench maxing, you know? I think you can kind of overfit onto certain distributions, and it won't be reflective of how well you generalize, right? Because easy ways to do this are, you take a benchmark and you just find very, very, very similar types of instances to the benchmark and you overtrain on these instances.

items.question: How do you see the current state of AI model evaluation?
items.object: The AI evaluation crisis and Codex-assisted evaluation development
items.answer: The other scary thing in the field is the number of canonical gold standard benchmarks is low. And we really are kind of in an evals crisis, right? Where all the really great evals that we all know, like growing up, like taking the SAT, those are all fully saturated. And we really need to find good new ways to benchmark the models. I think one great thing about tools like Codex is they really enabled the fast iteration of evals. We're able to just kind of have one person very quickly put together a very high-quality eval.

So, in many of the hard math and science evals, we've partnered with external organizations and they've been able to craft gold standards there for us. So, I think there's an interesting philosophy of separating the teams that are creating the evals from the teams that are optimizing the models themselves. Because that way you don't incentivize them, right? The way the evals team can work is they're trying to build evals that are hard for the models. So, there's this inherently adversarial process where you're not kind of cheating yourself. The incentives are somewhat aligned in the right way between the two teams.

Or certain capabilities that we want. And every capability on the foot side is an eval, right? You need some kind of eval that measures if you elicited exactly what you want and you want it well. So, yeah, it takes a lot of steering and just to get everyone on the same page with evals is also a lot of tough work.

items.question: What’s an example of humor from Yacoub, with whom you jointly manage research efforts, that you found very funny?

items.question: How do you understand the jagged frontier where AI models excel at some tasks but struggle with tasks humans find intuitive?
items.object: The jagged frontier of AI model capabilities relative to humans
items.answer: I mean, ultimately, I think what's intuitive for the models is often not that intuitive for the humans. There's a lot made of this jagged frontier analogy where there's some things that the models just inherently, based on maybe the data it sees or the things that we can teach it more easily, it's just good at. I actually think a lot of it boils down to also just context, right? The models don't have a lot of context. Vision, of course, is something that's more naturally biologically wired for humans. And so, I think there are just certain kind of jagged capabilities that models are better at than humans and vice versa. But I also think context, just being able to take a single task, learn lessons from it, and apply them to future tasks, that capability is something that a lot of people in AI are working towards right now. But it's very natural for humans.

items.question: How do you think about increasing a model’s context window as a way to enable long-horizon learning?
items.object: Long-context approaches to long-horizon learning and compaction
items.answer: I think there's kind of the canonical way you would solve for very long horizon learning, which is, you just naively increase your context window, right? And that makes sense. I think there's a difference between implementing long context and implementing long context well. And there is a lot of needle-in-a-haystack style evaluations to measure that. But I do think beyond that, there are also a lot of, in some sense, engineering and research shortcuts that you could take. So, many coding products today have features like compaction, right? Where you can compress kind of either insights or working state and stuff like that. It just shortcuts a lot of the very brutally difficult and expensive primitives that you have to build with just native long context.

items.question: How do you think about the opportunity for major new AI research bets as models approach the ability to conduct self-sustaining research?
items.object: The window for major new AI research bets before models can conduct self-sustaining research
items.answer: I feel like there are new bets, but probably not that many. In some sense, hopefully you feel like AGI is coming soon, right? And I think everyone sees that these models are getting really capable, and I think if you really imagine the implications of that, we're getting closer and closer to a world where the models can come up with more of the innovation. If they can kind of do self-sustaining research, this is one of the big goals that we've set for our research work. And so I think what really matters is are there big bets before that point in time? And I think the window is small, but there are still some pretty significant ideas we're trying out.

items.question: How do you view the claim that reaching AGI requires two or three more breakthroughs, such as continual learning?
items.object: The idea that reaching AGI requires several more breakthroughs, such as continual learning

I think we're trying a lot in the limitations of it. I don't know what I would consider as a breakthrough versus not, but I think there are clearly many shots on goal, and I'm pretty sure they'll work.

items.question: Why do you favor keeping image, audio, video, and text models under as few architectures as possible in a research lab?
items.object: Unifying image, audio, video, and text models under a shared architecture
items.answer: Well, yeah. I mean, I think for a research lab, I think there are a lot of advantages for it to be under one. You just have to maintain one infrastructure stack, for instance. I think the cost of maintaining and scaling many infrastructure stacks at once is something that you shouldn't underestimate. So, I think there are a lot of benefits to just, you know, you do some core research in your fundamental stack and that just carries over to whatever modality or whatever thing that you want. So, I think there's a strong bias for us to keep it in as few different architectures as possible.

items.question: How do you see the balance between human research taste and model execution shaping the future of AI-assisted research?
items.object: AI-assisted research and the role of research taste
items.answer: I think we're actually moving towards this world very quickly, right? I think both at OpenAI and our other labs, you're starting to see a lot of the work become mostly orchestration-focused, right? Like the researchers coming up with the ideas and the model's great enough to do the implementation execution by itself. So, when it comes down to, is the value coming up with ideas versus execution? Both are still important, but I just feel like there's this market shift towards just kind of being able to come up with a lot of ideas and then the model can actually do the execution and orchestration for you. So, I think it's going to be the future of doing research. We also said earlier, you know, the models don't quite have the taste yet. And that's why you still need the researchers coming up with the ideas. It's going to be hard to teach the models good taste. We noticed that, but in terms of actually accelerating the research, there's clear tangible benefits already.

items.question: Do you think AI models will ever match humans in research taste?
items.object: AI models developing research taste and doing end-to-end research
items.answer: I think so. I mean, when we look at our three-year roadmap, the end goal that we want to reach is one where the models are just doing end-to-end research. And I think a part of that problem is just being able to have the model come up with good taste. You point at some generic benchmark or something and it finds the right solutions.

items.question: How do you think OpenAI should handle high-risk research bets that don't pan out?
items.object: OpenAI’s approach to failed high-risk research bets
items.answer: Well, I would say that is a big part of OpenAI's alpha because I think one thing that differentiates us from other labs is we take a lot of high-risk bets. And I think that's what's allowed us to stay at the frontier so consistently over time. But it also means that some of the bets are not going to pan out. And a hard corollary of that is when a bet doesn't pan out, you have to not delude yourself into thinking that this is something that will work and disconnect from it. So, I think there are certain calls that you have to make, right? Like, look back and be like, well, this was a promising idea at the time, but actually it's less important than we thought; there's some other approach that works better or there's something else that we discovered. But I think much of that work is also very fruitful. So, what we realized is even sometimes when people fail at proving out a technique, their write-ups are very important because they'll often be a natural idea and you can perhaps save a lot of people from going through the same pain.

items.question: How do you evaluate a researcher whose high-risk research bets repeatedly fail to pan out?
items.object: Evaluating researchers whose high-risk research bets repeatedly fail
items.answer: Just through experience, I've definitely seen some people fall into this. But I've also had several cases where it's just bet after bet, it doesn't pan out, and just when you're at the brink of frustration, you have something that's a mega hit. And this happened enough, so it really just depends on whether the ideas themselves are sound. They could be ambitious, but they still have to be sound. And there's a certain kind of person who will just take a lot of those ideas, and it's okay because they're somewhat on the riskier frontier. But they only have to justify it once in a while for it to make sense, right? It may be like a very trading-like kind of lens on the world, but it's just on our expectation, right? They need to add value.
